canberra.title: Weirdness unleashed at the National Portrait Gallery
canberra.snippet: Get ready for things to get wonderfully weird at the National Portrait Gallery these school holidays. Whether your household spent the ea...
canberra.content:
The National Portrait Gallery invites you to enter the world of Andy Griffiths, master of pure, unadulterated nonsense. Photo: NPG.

Get ready for things to get wonderfully weird at the National Portrait Gallery these school holidays.

Whether your household spent the early years devouring The Day My Bum Went Psycho or obsessing over The 13-Storey Treehouse, one of Australia’s most iconic storytellers is officially taking over Canberra’s premier hall of faces.

Unveiling late this month, a major new 3D-printed portrait of Australian Children’s Laureate Andy Griffiths is setting up shop at the Gallery — and he isn’t coming alone.

Accompanying the surreal sculpture by artist Ronnie van Hout is a portal straight into Griffiths’ creative vault, launching with a massive (and blissfully free) family day.

Griffiths is one of Australia’s most beloved authors and his books have topped the New York Times bestseller list, scooped up 80 children’s choice awards, morphed into an animated TV series and moved a staggering 13 million copies across Australia and New Zealand.

The portrait itself — a kaleidoscopic, “surreal collision of punk rock aesthetics and childhood imagination” is a fittingly unconventional collision of two of Australia and New Zealand’s most irreverent creative minds.

In the large-scale sculpture, a standing Andy holds two mini-me versions in his hand, while a fourth Andy gazes down at himself from the branches of a tree in a nod to his famous Treehouse series.

“This is a commission that challenges conventional expectations of portraiture because it really extends beyond pure likeness … It’s a place where fact, fiction, and portraiture collide,” Gallery Senior Curator Serena Bentley says.

“Both Griffiths and van Hout have this real kinship around music, particularly an interest in punk music and the sentiments of punk, and fuse their respective practices — particularly the sentiments of being transgressive, pushing the boundaries, creating work where anything goes, and where difference is promoted and accepted.”

Before you even lay eyes on the commission, however, you enter the warm-up act: the “Brainstorm” space.

Visitors will also meet the artist whose surreal works make weird look effortless — Ronnie van Hout. Photo: NPG.

An interactive gateway into the writer’s brain, this dedicated interactive space features more than 130 books, toys and curiosities that have fuelled Griffiths’ unique brand of creativity.

“It’s a space that’s about entering into Andy Griffiths’ mind to get some understanding of where ideas or inspiration comes from,” Bentley explains.

To curate it, gallery staff, Griffiths, and his partner Jill spent hours sifting through the op-shop finds and weird relics the author has assembled in his personal writing room over the years.

“For him, how you might assemble these little objects in new and unexpected ways has been a means of generating ideas,” Bentley says. “By the end of the day, we were in this really interesting rhythm where we were assembling objects, and I don’t know how you can articulate why a banana with eyes, a ball of fingers and a Godzilla with a baby’s head works together, but it just does.”

The public is invited to celebrate the new portrait and interactive space at the Gallery’s annual family day, Art.Make.Create, timed for the school holidays.

Billed as a “seriously silly day,” this celebration of creativity, imagination and storytelling leans hard into Griffiths’ trademark brand of chaotic creativity.

Presiding over the official unveiling will be Griffiths and van Hout themselves, in conversation with gallery director Bree Pickering.

Afterwards, Griffiths will lead a session packed with stories, banter, laughter and a book signing.

“That will be a high-energy, interactive session to get everyone laughing and in the mood for a super silly day,” gallery program development lead Ellie Brotchie says. “Definitely bring your Andy books in to be signed.”

Longtime Griffiths illustrator Bill Hope will also host live drawing workshops and creative portraiture demonstrations. Visitors can wander over to the Scribbletorium — a Treehouse-inspired room where scribbling on (almost) every surface isn’t just allowed, it’s encouraged.

Rounding out the day is a book swap, temporary tattoo stations, interactive tours, live rock ‘n’ roll from Bunny Racket, food trucks and a dedicated quiet hour from 3 to 4 pm.

“We want people to walk away feeling inspired and encouraged to celebrate being a little weird, a little silly,” Brotchie says. “And to know that creativity looks different for everyone. There’s no shortage of ideas, or ways to express them. We hope we can cultivate that.”

The portrait of Andy Griffiths and Brainstorm: Inside the Mind of Andy Griffiths space will be on display through to mid-2027. Andy Griffiths: art.make.create will be held on Saturday 26 September, and some activities continue throughout the September school holidays.

canberra.title: Why St Clare’s is ripe for a co-ed future
canberra.snippet: St Clare’s College is resisting suggestions that it open its doors to boys, but single-sex schools are on the wane and the Griffith...
canberra.content:
St Clare’s College in Griffith is well under capacity. Photo: Claire Fenwicke.

St Clare’s College is resisting suggestions that it open its doors to boys, but single-sex schools are on the wane and the Griffith school is well below capacity despite growing demand for Catholic education in the region.

The body charged with running the region’s Catholic schools, Catholic Archdiocese of Canberra and Goulburn Education Limited (CACGEL), is considering a move to co-ed for St Clare’s as CACGEL faces the dilemma of growing demand in a tightening financial environment.

Its Apostolic Action Plan has identified a gap in coverage on Canberra’s southside, but there is minimal land available for the establishment of new schools.

CACGEL is therefore looking to develop precincts to pool resources, particularly in the Queanbeyan-Inner South area which would form a Cathedral Precinct.

A discussion paper released this week (15 September) ahead of public consultation notes that St Clare’s has a capacity of 1200 students but has only 864 enrolled.

In contrast, feeder primary schools in the proposed precinct are booming. St Gregory’s in Queanbeyan is at capacity with 737 students enrolled at the school across Kindergarten to Year 6, and increasing numbers of families are also seeking enrolment at St Benedict’s in Narrabundah.

The discussion paper says including St Gregory’s in the precinct could offer a K-12 pathway for both boys and girls, if St Clare’s became a co-ed school and there was an enhanced partnership with St Edmund’s College.

Feedback from a survey of K-5 parents indicated strong support for establishing new co-ed secondary colleges in the south of Canberra.

“This appears to mirror broader trends in parent preference for co-education,” the paper says.

“Given these trends, the costs of building new schools, and the capacity at St Clare’s College, there is an open question for CACGEL about whether the system currently has a sustainable mix in two single-sex girls’ colleges and three co-educational colleges or whether another combination of colleges may reflect a more contemporary model for the future.”

The paper says that considering a co-ed future for St Clare’s was not a criticism of it but part of how CACGEL could best respond to parent choice, changing demographics and the emerging and future needs of families across the Archdiocese.

It notes St Clare’s central location, comparatively large footprint and floor area with capacity for 1200, softer enrolment demand, and the prospective pathways for students from within the Cathedral Precinct, particularly for families in the Queanbeyan and surrounding areas.

Any change would not happen before 2028 and be staged over a number of years after extensive consultation with the community.

Expanding capacity at Merici College in the inner north would also have to be on the table to cater for those families in Canberra who will continue to seek a single-sex girls’ education.

The discussion paper also covers potential sites for new schools in Queanbeyan and Molonglo, extending the capacity of St Mary MacKillop College and a potential precinct in Weston Creek, where two primary schools – St Jude’s in Holder and St John Vianney in Warramanga – could become secondary schools.

It identifies significant population growth and demand for Catholic education in the newly established suburbs of the Molonglo Valley. The school age population (5–17 years) in the Molonglo Valley is forecast to increase by 8 per cent annually between 2026 and 2036, with the secondary school age population expected to reach 3,500 students by 2036.

A 5ha parcel of land in Stromlo Reach is slated for release before 2030, the first of the three sites to be made available for a non-government school.

The paper says it is anticipated that the site will be for a primary school, but it is also possible it may be large enough to establish a year 7-12 college.

It says a primary school will increase pressure for another secondary Catholic school option in the region but a secondary school would open up the opportunity to establish another multi-school precinct in the south-west of Canberra, potentially involving St Jude’s and St John Vianney and possibly others feeding into a Stromlo Reach Catholic co-education college.

This could include expanding one of these schools to become a P-12 school or a 7-12 college to give all students within the precinct a P-12 pathway.

Families can have their say by emailing the School Community Consultation – community.consultation.scc@cg.catholic.edu.au – or by completing a School Community Consultation Survey that will be released this month or a School Community Consultation session.

canberra.title: The Braddon carwash that accidentally became a cultural icon
canberra.snippet: It’s hard to think of a Canberra suburb that’s seen more change than Braddon. The once semi-industrial precinct, where 20 years ago you w...
canberra.content:
Waves carwash is doing its bit in keeping Braddon cool. Photo: Tenele Conway.

It’s hard to think of a Canberra suburb that’s seen more change than Braddon. The once semi-industrial precinct, where 20 years ago you were more likely to get your car serviced than find a good meal, has spent the past two decades evolving into Canberra’s most sought-after food and entertainment mecca.

But as apartment and commercial developments become increasingly upmarket, Braddon risks reaching a point of no return.

The grit and countercultural vibes that make the suburb worth visiting are slowly being devoured by progress, while the bootstrapped businesses Canberrans have embraced risk being squeezed out by rising rents.

It’s an evolution that Adrian Sacco, director of Waves Carwash, has witnessed firsthand with his carwash becoming an unlikely champion for small business with his growing collection of food trucks squeezed in around the spray guns and curtain scrubbers.

“We were originally inspired by the Hamlet that opened up across the road in 2014, which created a lot of momentum for food trucks; they were the pioneers of this, and it was the advent of permanent food trucks in Braddon,” Adrian tells Region.

The Hamlet was Braddon’s OG food truck village. Photo: This is Canberra.

With momentum building and the Hamlet only ever being a temporary food village, in 2018 Adrian started inviting food trucks to the Waves Carwash site on Friday and Saturday nights, with the schedule being publicly available through a Facebook page called Braddon Food Trucks.

“It was an opportunity to do something a little different and give back to the community with some new food options,” Adrian explains.

“The weekend events allowed food vendors to dip their toes in the water and leverage the excitement for food trucks in the area.”

The weekend pop-ups proved to Adrian that the demand from the community was there and, leveraging his background in property development, he could see that they could be utilising the large Waves Carwash corner site more effectively.

“Our site would often become a car park with people illegally parking in the driveway, and that wasn’t ideal for us. When I did my Masters of Property at university, we talked about additional use of the land beyond the existing.”

BanMe owners Minh Tri Nguyen and Kathy Phan in their Braddon store onsite at Waves Carwash. Photo: Kazuri Photography.

This idea jump-started the inclusion of permanent food trucks on the site and, some might say, the rest is history.

Since then Adrian has pushed the site to capacity with the building now surrounded on multiple sides, including on the rear driveway where Moowing Steak and Bella Pizza have most recently set up shop.

Adrian’s pricing structure has formed a stepping stone for businesses to go from operating from a food truck to a bricks and mortar shopfront, some with him and some being able to establish themselves and open elsewhere in Canberra.

“As the suburb gentrified, spaces where we had ancillary motor vehicle tenants like Avis and Budget became available, and we have now filled them with great food options.”

Little Phat Rolls opened at Waves in 2022. Photo: Lucy Ridge.

When Adrian talks about great food options, he’s underselling it. The hub is home to some of the city’s most exciting multicultural eats.

In prime position on the front corner, Yaka on Wheels serves complex Sri Lankan dishes, while long-time resident Tikka Stand specialises in Indian street food and freshly grilled meats. Little Phat Rolls offers Vietnamese soups and bánh mì, as does BanMe in one of the commercial spaces.

PJ’s Kebabs has late-night cravings covered until midnight seven days a week, Bella pumps out 24-hour fermented sourdough pizzas, and right next door, Moowing Steak serves grain-fed ribeye that might just change your expectations of food truck dining.

canberra.title: The Canberra Bookshelf: When remarkable women took a seat the table, but not on the throne
canberra.snippet: Two books recognised in this year’s Children’s Book Council of Australia Book of the Year Awards have appeared in earlier editions ...
canberra.content:
Eleri Harris cleverly combines levity and gravitas in her history of the first women in Federal Parliament.

Two books recognised in this year’s Children’s Book Council of Australia Book of the Year Awards have appeared in earlier editions of this column: Younger Readers Honour Book Sandy Bigna for Little Bones (UQP) and Eve Pownall Award winners Stephanie Owen Reeder and Ingrid Bartowiak for Peculiar Parents (NLA Publishing).

Author-illustrator Eleri Harris was awarded the Eve Pownall Honour Book for A Loo of One’s Own (Allen & Unwin, Australia 2026). The book provides a history of some of the less illustrious aspects of our national parliament and its persistent misogyny/patriarchy.

The text recounts the experience of the first two women elected to Federal Parliament, Dorothy Tangney and Enid Lyons. This was in 1943.

These very capable women entered a parliament which was very much an old boys’ club. However, although other women worked in the building in many capacities, no toilet facilities were provided for women. Astoundingly, it was not until 1974 that the government finally created a women’s toilet!

Eleri Harris has illustrated this interesting history in an Art Deco style appropriate to the time of women’s entry into Federal Parliament, but both the style and tone are also decidedly modern, cleverly combining levity and gravitas.

We are left in no doubt about the contribution (beyond toilets) that these and other women made to our democracy – and indeed how far we are yet to go in this regard.

The CBCA judges describe Eleri’s palette and composition as “confident”, and her take on the period as “irreverent 21st century breeziness”. They say that she brings a “unique blend of sharp observation and sense of fun” to the genre and hope that this continues in a long list of picture books to come.

Irene Wettenhall’s collection of eight poems explores an ancestor’s migration from England and the author’s need to uncover her past.

On the subjects of remarkable women and history, The Mary Poems by Irene Wettenhall (Independently published, 2026) is an affecting imagining of the life and thoughts of the poet’s ancestor, Mary Burgess Wettenhall née Bussell (1809 to 1896).

This delicate collection of eight poems traces key parts of Mary’s life, from leaving her native village of Paul in Cornwall in 1835 with her husband as emigrants to Van Diemen’s Land, to the author’s own voyage to England and Scotland in 2025 in search of her ancestry.

Period photographs accompany the poems and offer a moving expression not only of Mary’s life and feelings as imagined by her current-day relative, but also of the author’s need to uncover her past and consider her own mortality.

Irene has drawn on some family history material in selecting key moments in Mary’s life, but it is the sympathetic touch, the fellow feeling of one woman to another, shown in her words, that lends such power to these word pictures:

Our silver polished, the trunks were packed:

Bibles and hymn books, seeds for a garden

Wordsworth and Austen, the linen

Pressed and folded with lavender,

…

I woke up on the other side of the world.

The poet takes the words far beyond documentary poetry, into a category the works could be classified as. They clearly show Irene’s ability to identify with her ancestor, and with this woman’s hopes and fears as her life changed so radically in the wake of her husband’s war service.

When the Royal Navy scaled down after the Napoleonic Wars, her husband was laid off on half pay and encouraged to emigrate. At the time, the prospects looked rosy, but things turned sour as economic recession hit in the 1840s.

Irene refers us to the words of Jordie Albiston:

One must allow oneself to be moved, to feel the breath, to see the most trivial moments as moments in a life.

And this is indeed what Irene does so beautifully here. And hence, so does the reader. The book is a disciplined collection which perfectly achieves its goal.

Barbie Robinson is co-founder and a content creator for Living Arts Canberra, a not-for-profit media outfit supporting arts and community in the Canberra region and books worldwide through its website, podcast interviews and a 24/7 internet radio station, at Living Arts Canberra.

canberra.title: ‘I can actually see myself’: Canberra tour guide awarded national honour
canberra.snippet: After three years in the profession, a Canberra tour guide’s latest honour has come during a national competition. Angie Ouyang joi...
canberra.content:
19 September 2026

Start the conversation

Angie Ouyang says she aims to make her tours “memorable” by finding common ground with visitors. Photo: Supplied.

After three years in the profession, a Canberra tour guide’s latest honour has come during a national competition.

Angie Ouyang joined the National Museum of Australia in 2023 and has worked as a host ever since.

The thought of talking to groups of strangers might make you break out in a cold sweat, but Angie has come to love it.

She also admits that she’s “always a bit nervous” before a tour.

“But every time, it’s always finished well,” she said.

“In this job, I can use my language skills. I can meet people, and I can learn and share [information].”

Despite her short time in the field, Angie took home bronze in the Australian Top Tour Guide Awards earlier this week.

It follows her previous win as Top Tour Guide in the Canberra Region.

Each day Angie runs multiple guided tours, covering things like the museum’s design, First Nations history and dedicated exhibitions.

She runs her tours to connect with visitors.

“I would ask what might interest you,” she said when asked about her approach.

“If they say, ‘I’m interested in painting’, I would take note of all those paintings from my tour … I adapt to the visitors’ needs.

“It’s a long process!”

While Canberra’s winter mornings are “not that much” warmer than the South Pole, she said the museum’s Antarctica exhibition was one of her favourites to talk about with visitors.

“I’ve done all those three daily tours … Sometimes I’ll be requested to do some special tours, like the Our Story exhibition for the VIP tour.”

Angie says leading tours through the NMA’s current Antarctica exhibition has been a career highlight. Photo: Jarryd Rowley.

Working at the museum was her first job in Australia after she immigrated from China.

Before arriving in the bush capital, she had worked as a French teacher at the University of Guangzhou.

“[Since I started] at the National Museum of Australia, I understand Australian history so much better, and I can actually see myself, my place in Australian history as an immigrant.

“That’s the motivation.

“I want to share these experiences and help people to connect more with Australian history.”

Angie said the award process was “like doing a tour” through her career for the judges, and involved filling an entry form, a written submission and a 30-minute interview.

“It was like guiding them [through] my journey, and it’s very fun,” she said of the experience.

“I just cared that I had done my best.”

Angie remembers her fellow hosts and other museum staff as cheering her on when she found out she’d won.

“I received so much encouragement and support … There are so many great guys in our museum.

“I’m representing them. I feel very honoured and lucky.”

Canberra Region Tourism Industry Council Managing Director Debra Beetham paid tribute to Angie’s win.

“We are proud to see the Canberra Region Tour Guide Award winner Angie Ouyang take out Bronze at the Australian Top Tour Guide Awards; it is a testament to her passion and the stories she shares every day.”

The NMA is open daily 9 am to 5 pm (except Christmas Day).

australia.title: Shark catch-and-kill order issued after swimmer dies off popular Perth beach
australia.snippet: Man, 63, fatally bitten by shark at Sorrento beach on Friday morning Get our breaking news email , free app or daily news podcast A shark...
australia.content:
A shark that fatally attacked a man on a beach in Perth’s north will be “destroyed” if it is captured, after an order was issued by the Western Australian government.

As the hunt for the animal remained under way on Saturday, the WA fisheries minister, Jackie Jarvis, revealed she had greenlit the order.

“Given the shark had been positively identified, remained in the vicinity following a fatal attack and was considered to pose an ongoing threat, I authorised fisheries officers to destroy the shark if captured,” she said in a social media post.

Emergency services were called to the popular Sorrento beach at about 10.30am on Friday after reports of a shark-related incident.

Western Australia police said a 63-year-old man had been bitten by a shark while swimming along the coast. He died as a result of his injuries, police said.

Emergency services, including water and air personnel, conducted an extensive search of the area. The swimmer’s body had not been found.

Water police requested the shark be captured to assist with the recovery of potential coronial evidence.

Police and fisheries officials remained in the area and nearby beaches were closed.

“My deepest condolences are with the family and loved ones of the 63-year-old man who tragically lost his life at Sorrento Beach yesterday,” Jarvis said.

“This is an incredibly sad and distressing incident and my thoughts are with everyone involved.”

Locals were urged to stay out of the water until the beach was declared safe for swimming.

The local state MP, Liam Staltari, extended his condolences to the man’s family, friends and loved ones.

“Like all locals and people from across WA, I’m deeply saddened by the tragic death of a man following today’s shark attack at Sorrento beach,” he said.

“Our entire community is thinking of you at this incredibly difficult time.”

A witness, Darrel Haythornthwaite, told 7News that he could not believe the incident had occurred, “especially in a place like this”. He said the man’s friend, who was swimming with him, made it back to shore but was inconsolable.

“He felt bad because he didn’t go back to save his mate and I said, ‘Nah you couldn’t have done that’,” he told the outlet. “There’s nothing that anyone could have done.”

Another witness, Ingrid Mitchell, told 9News she swam at the beach every day and did not expect sharks to attack outside dawn and dusk.

“There was other swimmers in there … just near the seaweed, and there was one poor girl there who was sunbaking, and she saw the whole lot as well,” she said.

A third witness, Jacqui Rapaic, told the ABC she was walking along the beach with a friend when the incident occurred.

“My friend said, ‘Jac, I think there’s been a shark attack,’ and I looked out to the ocean and I could see a pool of blood,” she said.

“I hugged on to my friend … [we] felt rather traumatised at that point. It happened so quickly.”

The fatality followed a shark attack on Monday at the remote Glenfield beach, north of Geraldton on WA’s mid-west coast, which left a surfer with serious injuries.

He was taken to the nearby Geraldton health campus and was in a stable condition.

– with AAP

australia.title: ’National pride’ and ‘Western values’ the focus of Coalition education plan that would reduce First Nations content
australia.snippet: Curriculum proposal, unveiled by shadow education minister Julian Leeser, would also cut content about sustainability and Australia’s eng...
australia.content:
Content on Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander histories and culture, Australia’s engagement with Asia, and sustainability would be cut from the Australian curriculum under a Coalition plan to teach students about “national pride” and “Western values”.

The shadow education minister, Julian Leeser, revealed during a speech delivered to an education conference on Saturday in Sydney that the Coalition would remove the three cross-curriculum priorities.

According to the Australian curriculum, the priorities – which are not separate subjects – allow students to engage with and better understand their world by providing opportunities to enrich the content of other subjects like English, history and science.

But Leeser claimed these priorities “almost by definition [mean] they’re not being taught by people with subject matter expertise” and did both the topics and teachers a disservice.

He said they should instead be delivered as discrete, planned topics within history, geography or science classes.

“If you’re teaching a maths or science or history class, I’d like you not to have to worry about incorporating those additional bits,” he said.

As part of the Coalition’s curriculum reform proposal, Leeser also said students should be taught and exposed to the “foundations of Western culture” including democracy, the rule of law and “a fair go”.

“I want Australian students to learn more about all three strands of our history: our Indigenous heritage, our British foundation and our multicultural character,” he said.

“Let every school have a flag and let every student take pride in it, its history and the values for which it stands.

“On teaching our children about national pride, there is much to do.”

Meanwhile, One Nation’s current education platform states “there should be no room for Western, white, gender, guilt shaming in any classroom”.

As the Coalition attempts to win back voters from One Nation, their policy commits to streamlining pathways to make it easier for mid-career Australians to pivot to teaching, addressing student behaviour, reducing screen time and AI use, and lifting educational outcomes for boys.

The 2025 Programme for International Student Assessment results, released earlier this month, found Australia had dropped to its worst ever results for maths and reading, and that classroom disruption remained among the worst in the world.

Leeser floated the idea of helping veterans become teachers.

“When I think about the need for better classroom behaviour and more discipline in our classrooms, about the need for more support for Australian values, it seems to make sense,” he said.

He claimed Labor was “only for public schools, but we are for all schools”.

“We need to stop class war politics and recognise that school funding is about funding for students, wherever they learn,” he said. “It’s time to restore excellence to Australian schools.”

australia.title: Tasmanian justice department review under way after AI and fake citation used in murderer’s parole decision
australia.snippet: Parole condition of convicted killer Susan Neill-Fraser deemed invalid after board cited non-existent case law Get our breaking news emai...
australia.content:
A review of potential artificial intelligence use in parole decisions will be undertaken after a “concerning” error in the case of a high-profile murderer.

Tasmania’s justice department on Friday evening confirmed the review was occurring, four days after a parole condition of convicted killer Susan Neill-Fraser was deemed invalid.

Neill-Fraser was released on parole in 2022 after serving 13 years behind bars for murdering her partner Bob Chappell on their yacht in 2009.

The state Parole Board later added conditions preventing her from speaking to the media to claim her innocence or an alleged wrongful conviction.

On Tuesday, after a legal challenge from Neill-Fraser, the supreme court of Tasmania ruled the condition was invalid and made without procedural fairness.

It was revealed in court that the Parole Board relied on a document prepared with the help of AI and cited case law that didn’t exist.

“The department will undertake a review to determine the extent to which artificial intelligence may have been used to inform past Tasmanian Parole Board decisions,” a justice department spokesperson said.

“The department is unable to comment further while the review is in progress.”

The Parole Board is an independent decision-making body to the department.

Prisoners Legal Service Tasmania chair Greg Barns said the conditions placed on Neill-Fraser were deeply troubling, and it was extraordinary that the case law relied on wasn’t checked.

The legal service was undertaking its own audit of two years’ worth of Parole Board decisions to see if there were any signs of AI use or mistakes, Barns said.

Sarah Schwartz, from the Human Rights Law Centre, which represented Neill-Fraser, said the case had revealed serious deficiencies.

“It’s really concerning that the Parole Board of Tasmania … used AI in generating this document,” she said outside court on Tuesday.

“[It] severely restricted our client’s fundamental freedoms, her freedom to speak in regard to her matter.”

A spokesperson for the Parole Board has said it does not comment on individual matters and was unable to answer questions about the extent of its AI use.

Neill-Fraser, who has launched multiple failed appeals against her conviction, has vowed to continue her fight to clear her name.

The state attorney general, Guy Barnett, has written to the Parole Board asking for an explanation and said the mistake was unacceptable.

australia.title: ‘Stunning backflip’: NSW opposition criticised for pledge to scrap gun buyback scheme if elected
australia.snippet: Liberals’ vow to scrap firearm ownership caps criticised by NSW police minister Yasmin Catley, who says plan would leave more guns in cir...
australia.content:
The New South Wales opposition plans, if elected next year, to freeze the state’s gun buyback scheme and unwind key firearms restrictions introduced after the Bondi beach terror attack.

NSW will become the first state to undertake Australia’s biggest gun buyback in 30 years, with the scheme set to begin on 2 November, providing compensation to licence holders for firearms under new ownership limits and the reclassification of certain weapons.

The Liberal opposition voted with the NSW government last year in support of a buyback, but now pledges it will scrap Labor’s firearm ownership caps for primary producers.

The state opposition leader, Kellie Sloane, on Saturday unveiled the Liberals’ plan to tackle firearms crime, proposing a commission of inquiry into gun laws and a freeze of the buyback while it completed its work.

“Following the inquiry, any buyback will be better targeted, provide fair compensation and allow associated ammunition and accessories to be surrendered in the same transaction,” Sloane said.

The NSW minister for police and counter-terrorism, Yasmin Catley, fired back at the Liberals’ plan, calling it a “stunning backflip” that would leave more guns in circulation and unwind key community safety protections.

Those protections were put in place after the worst terror attack in NSW in which 15 people were shot dead at Bondi beach on 14 December, 2025, at a Hanukah celebration.

Catley accused the Liberals and Nationals of following One Nation and putting politics before public safety.

“On an issue as serious as gun safety, the Coalition has gone from supporting stronger laws after Bondi to promising to unwind them as One Nation campaigns for them to be repealed,” she said in a statement.

“Our position is simple and it has not and will not change: fewer dangerous guns in circulation means a safer NSW.”

Sloane accused Labor of rushing through complex legislation without properly consulting licensed firearm owners, farmers, sporting shooters, collectors, firearms businesses and other affected stakeholders.

Sloane said the Liberals’ plan aimed to combat threats to community safety: organised crime, gangland violence, terrorism, firearms trafficking and illegal guns.

“We will fix Labor’s flawed laws and back our police with the powers and resources they need,” Sloane said.

The Liberals’ plan includes increased funding for the NSW firearms registry and relevant police commands to disrupt criminal networks, seize illegal firearms and combat gangland violence.

The maximum penalty for trafficking firearms would also be increased from 20 years’ jail to life imprisonment, with mandatory jail terms for carrying illegal guns.

australia.title: NSW council left without a mayor after names ‘drawn out of a hat’ in election tie-break bungle
australia.snippet: Clarence Valley councillor incorrectly elected after random draw that should have eliminated him Get our breaking news email , free app o...
australia.content:
A local council in northern New South Wales is without a mayor after a bungled election tie-break meant a candidate whose name was drawn “out of a hat” was wrongly told he had lost.

Clarence Valley councillors Peter Johnstone and Ray Smith were tied on votes for mayor after a ballot of other councillors this week.

The council’s general manager, Laura Black, then told them they would both have their names written on pieces of paper, and a random draw would determine the victor.

But shortly before drawing the name, Black wrongly declared that whoever she picked would be eliminated.

Smith’s name was pulled out, and Johnstone incorrectly elected mayor.

NSW local government laws stipulate that if there is a tie for votes between two remaining mayoral candidates, “the one elected is to be chosen by lot”.

The council said in a statement released on Friday: “Prior to the draw taking place, the General Manager, Laura Black, mistakenly advised those present that the councillor whose name was drawn would be eliminated. Cr Smith’s name was subsequently drawn and, based on that advice, Cr Johnstone was declared Mayor.”

“Council has sought urgent confirmation from the Office of Local Government regarding the appropriate remedial action to address the error.

“Once advice has been received, Council will provide further public information regarding the outcome and required next steps.”

Johnstone has since resigned as mayor, pending another vote. He posted on social media that he expected that vote to occur on Friday afternoon, but it was deferred as the council continued to seek legal advice.

“For those who don’t know, there was a Mayoral election yesterday in Clarence Valley and I stood. Unfortunately, the final vote was 4 votes each for Ray and me which meant that it went down to names out of a hat,” he posted on Friday morning.

“In the early rounds of the vote, the name drawn out of the hat is eliminated and we were told this would be the case in this round, so when Ray’s name was drawn, I was announced the winner and chaired the rest of the meeting.

“However, the procedures state that the name drawn in the final round is the winner, not the one eliminated. So it should have been Ray declared the winner.”

Johnstone went on to say he was “planning to go to the beach today. Looking at the waves is very therapeutic!”

NSW local government laws state that “to choose a candidate by lot, the names of the candidates who have equal numbers of votes are written on similar slips of paper by the returning officer, the slips are folded by the returning officer so as to prevent the names being seen, the slips are mixed and one is drawn at random by the returning officer and the candidate whose name is on the drawn slip is chosen”.

Black, as general manager, was the returning officer.

Johnstone posted that he expected a new election to be held before 2 October. But he also told Guardian Australia on Saturday morning that the legal advice could mean Black’s declaration as the returning officer meant the decision was final – even though it was wrong.

Adding even more confusion to the election, Johnstone said it was not clear that a hat was in fact used to draw the names. He was at the back of the room and did not see the fateful vessel.

“I have a feeling – and they’ve used something like this before – that it was actually a small box, almost like a shoebox,” he said.

“It’s not actually a hat, that’s just a phrase.”

Smith was contacted for comment.

world.title: Men deported from US bound and beaten in Equatorial Guinea detention hotel, lawyers say
world.snippet: Group trapped at Hotel Bamy after US removal as rights groups sound alarm over poor conditions and violence Two men that the Trump admini...
world.content:
Two men that the Trump administration expelled to Equatorial Guinea were bound, fitted with bags over their heads, beaten and pushed down a flight of stairs, all in plain view of other US deportees, according to witnesses and human rights lawyers.

The men – one from Egypt and one from Eritrea – were then taken to a prison. About 30 detainees from the US remain trapped at a hotel in the outskirts of the coastal city of Malabo after being deported from the US. Detainees have said they believe the men were beaten for telling the press and human rights advocates about the poor conditions and violence inside the hotel, and that they are haunted by flashbacks and terrified they will be retaliated against next.

Human rights advocates and experts have warned for months that conditions at the Hotel Bamy – a run-down establishment that has served as a detention center for US deportees – are dangerous.

The US has sent at least 66 people from different African countries, Cuba and Brazil to Equatorial Guinea, which has received $7.5m as part of a deal to cooperate with the US deportation program. The Trump administration has pursued dozens of similar deals with countries to take in immigrants that the US cannot deport directly to their home countries, where judges have deemed they would face torture or persecution. In the past, the US government allowed those people to live and work in the US indefinitely.

The Trump administration, however, has sought instead to expel them to third countries where they have no ties, do not speak the local language and have no legal status – trapping them in limbo.

Advocates have been especially concerned for deportees sent to Equatorial Guinea, where the authoritarian government is notorious for human rights abuses, including torture, according to the US state department. Detainees held at Hotel Bamy have told the Guardian that armed guards keep watch over them 24/7, and that they have not been provided any medical care or even fresh clothes since arriving there. One of the detainees, who has a severe stomach hernia that requires visits to the hospital to drain his stomach due excessive fluid build-up, said he has been unable to see a doctor since arriving at Hotel Bamy.

Other detainees have managed to obtain medication for HIV, diabetes and other conditions via human rights lawyers, but remain fearful that access to medications will be arbitrarily cut off.

The two men who were tortured – Ahmed Soliman, 31, of Egypt, and Samson Birhane, 47, of Eritrea – have since been transferred to a prison in Malabo. Multiple witnesses recounted that the police officers shouted, “Where is the phone? Where is the phone!” as they beat the men, who had initially been accused of breaking a mirror at the hotel before they were pulled aside and arrested.

The beating, which occurred on 11 September, followed the release of a video first reported by Reuters showing conditions at the hotel and the violent behavior of the guards. The detainees had been using cellphones to communicate with lawyers and the media about the conditions they were facing.

In the video taken by Soliman, which lawyers shared with the Guardian, authorities are seen pointing guns at the deportees. A Cuban man asked the officer for the return of his confiscated mobile phone ​so he could contact relatives and a ​lawyer, but was ignored. When officers noticed Soliman filming the exchange with his mobile phone, multiple officers rushed at him and others standing nearby, pointed their guns, and told Soliman to remain on his knees with his hands up for 10-15 minutes.

In another video, Soliman was able to film authorities forcibly sending US deportees to Ethiopia, where they are likely to face torture. When deportees resisted going with authorities, officials gave them the option to “go back to their home country” or “go to prison”. At least 12 people have been returned by Equatorial Guinea to their home country, where they face persecution.

In May, human rights experts at the United Nations issued a rare public appeal asking Equatorial Guinea to halt plans to return deportees to their home countries and to comply with international human rights standards and avoid refoulement, or the expulsion of people to countries where they face persecution.

“This is a human rights catastrophe,” said Bella Mosselmans, director of the Global Strategic Litigation Council, who represents several of the deportees at Hotel Bamy. The US and Equatorial Guinea “must be held accountable for the atrocities they are committing”, she added.

In the week since Soliman and Birhane were beaten, police have also been searching the other detainees’ hotel rooms for cellphones, and have confiscated them. They have also barred lawyers from seeing the deportees. Authorities have told the 29 US deportees who remain at Hotel Bamy that they may never see Soliman or Birhane again, according to lawyers. One detainee who witnessed the beating said authorities treat them as if they are “blanks” who “don’t even exist”. Another detainee said an officer told her: “You will disappear from the earth. I am the law.”

Witnesses said they feared for the lives of Soliman and Birhane, who came to the US as children.

Soliman is a gay man from Egypt who had lived in Phoenix for most of his life. He had a green card, but lost status after he was convicted of drug possession. He served time for his crimes, and in October, a judge had determined he would face persecution and torture if he were to return to Egypt due to his sexuality.

Birhane had come to the US as a refugee when he was 13, but lost status after a conviction for robbery when he was in high school, in 1988. He was allowed to remain in the US after a judge ruled he faced torture in Eritrea, and had been regularly checking in with Immigration and Customs Enforcement as required.

Lawyers for the deportees shared copies of multiple emails they had sent to the US embassy in Equatorial Guinea alerting them to threats and violence against those detained at Hotel Bamy, but those messages have gone unanswered, they said. In July, amid a lawsuit challenging conditions for deportees, the African Commission issued an urgent interim order instructing the government of Equatorial Guinea to refrain from deporting, transferring, or relocating deportees against their will.

A spokesperson for Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) said that “when an individual is no longer in ICE custody, ICE is no longer responsible for them”, adding: “All of these illegal aliens were deported to a safe third country.” The agency did not engage with questions about the violence deportees have faced.

A spokesperson for the state department said: “The US government will use all legal means to remove those with no right to remain in our country.”

The agency did not respond to questions about whether it was aware of how Equatorial Guinea was treating US deportees, nor would it acknowledge whether any measures have been taken to intervene.

“As a general matter, we do not comment on the details of our private diplomatic communications with other governments,” the spokesperson said.

world.title: Survivors recount panic and struggle to breathe in Nigerian prison cell where 37 died
world.snippet: Police fire teargas as protests break out in city of Minna after deaths of suspected illegal goldminers, many of whom were children Survi...
world.content:
Survivors from a prison cell in Nigeria where 37 suspected illegal goldminers died while in the custody of a paramilitary group this week have recounted their panic and struggle for breath, as police on Friday fired teargas at people protesting against the deaths and imposed an overnight curfew in the city of Minna.

The victims – many of whom were children – were found dead on Thursday in the cells of the Nigeria Security and Civil Defence Corps (NSCDC), which had raided suspected illegal goldmines and ⁠locked up dozens of miners in the city, the state capital of the mineral-rich state of Niger.

NSCDC – a paramilitary group that works with police – initially blamed the deaths on a disease outbreak. However, an intelligence report seen by Agence France-Presse (AFP) said preliminary information suggested that overcrowding and inadequate ventilation were responsible.

The state governor, Umar Bago, said many of the dead were children, aged 14 to 18, who had been working in the mines instead of going to school. “There are issues of illegal mining and it is taking a toll on our children,” he said.

Dauda Shehu, a survivor from the cell, told journalists at a hospital on Friday: “We were jam-packed in the cell, no ventilation for us to breathe well. All of a sudden we realised that we could not breathe and we were all scampering for where to get fresh air, we even appealed to them several times, banged the cell door, but they refused to answer us.”

A video shared online showed the bodies of dozens of young men clad only in shorts, most of whom appeared to be teenagers, sprawled on the ground out in the open. Volunteers wearing gloves can be seen standing over the dead, while veiled women try to identify the bodies of their relatives. Voices shouting curses on those responsible can be heard in the background.

AFP reported that another survivor, who asked not to be named, said he had made it out alive because he was near the cell’s entrance, where he could breathe better. “We were screaming for help,” he said, with detainees telling the guards that “people are dying one after the other. They did not believe us.”

President Bola Ahmed Tinubu ordered an investigation into the deaths after his government earlier suspended some senior officials.

But protests over the deaths broke out on Thursday evening in Minna. On Friday dozens of young people, including miners and their relatives, gathered near the NSCDC’s office in the city. Police cordoned off the area and attempted to disperse the protesters by firing teargas.

A Reuters witness saw security forces fire live rounds as protesters – ​some armed with sticks, machetes and traditional hunting rifles – called ‌for justice. Some protesters tried ‌to set fire to government buildings in the Tunga neighbourhood. “We are not thieves – we are simply seeking a way to make ‌a living by mining,” Yusuf Auwal, a miner who joined the protesters, told Reuters. At least one body lay on the streets. Soldiers and police officers patrolled Minna to try to restore order.

As ⁠curfew began at 6pm local time on Friday, security forces appeared to have at least temporarily restored order to the streets of the city.

The NSCDC said the detainees had been held in raids on suspected illegal mines on 15 and 16 September in the Wushishi-Lukoto area west of Minna. Nigeria’s interior minister, Olubunmi Tunji-Ojo, ordered the immediate suspension of Niger state’s NSCDC commandant, Suberu Siyaka Aniviye, pending the outcome of an investigation.

Niger state, which is Nigeria’s largest and is more than twice the size of Belgium, is rich in minerals and attracts thousands of artisanal miners, most lured by gold.

Police and the NSCDC did not initially provide a precise number of deaths but the state governor, Mohammed Umaru Bago, later confirmed 37 people had died.

“It’s so sad, it’s so tragic,” he said, adding an inquiry into the deaths had already started work. He declared three days of mourning and postponed the start of campaigning for elections due in January. The men were buried on Thursday, according to Islamic tradition, without any forensic investigations.

The scramble for gold reserves dug up in illegal mines in Niger state is fuelling violence by criminal gangs, according to officials and experts. The gangs tax the miners and demand a cut from the extracted ore as a levy to allow them access to the pits.

Most of the illegally mined gold is smuggled to the United Arab Emirates, where it is laundered into the global supply chain in Europe, the US, Asia and South Africa, according to a 2024 Swissaid report.

Apart from gold, the state of Niger sits on deposits of other minerals including tantalite, copper and lithium, which are in strong demand for use in electric vehicles and clean energy technology.

Agence France-Presse and Reuters contributed to this report

world.title: British woman who was kidnapped in Malawi rescued by police after shootout
world.snippet: Four of Nurat Osman’s alleged abductors were killed during rescue after she was taken from outside her home last week A British woman kid...
world.content:
A British woman kidnapped in Malawi last week has been rescued by police after a shootout in which four of her alleged abductors were killed.

Nusrat Osman was abducted outside her home in the southern city of Blantyre on 11 September at about 12.30pm. Police had offered a reward of 30m Malawi kwacha (£12,950) for information leading to her rescue and the arrest of the perpetrators.

Malawian police announced Osman’s rescue late on Thursday in a statement. “There was an exchange of fire between police and kidnappers, who were armed with [an] AK47 rifle and a Girsan Regard MC pistol. In the process, the criminals got shot and were taken to hospital where they succumbed to their injuries.” it read.

A police officer, deputy inspector general Mlowoka Noel Kayira, was also shot during the operation. “He is currently receiving medical attention at the hospital and is in a stable condition,” police said.

Osman, a 47-year-old auditor and mother of two, was safe and “not too shaken” after her ordeal, her brother Shobi Jiwa told the Sun, expressing his gratitude to Malawi’s police.

Jiwa reserved special thanks for Kayira. “He is the hero of our family. He’s the hero of the country,” he said. “He’s the hero of the world, actually, for putting his life at risk and taking a bullet into himself for my sister.”

Kidnappings are rare in Malawi, which has experienced a rise in pickpocketing and house burglaries by often armed men in recent years amid unstable, crisis-ridden economic conditions.

The landlocked southern African country is one of the world’s poorest nations, with a population of about 22 million and an average annual income of just $672, according to the World Bank.

In 2024, a country report by the US state department’s diplomatic security service said: “Kidnappings are not a widespread concern in Malawi, and there have been no recent high-profile incidents involving westerners.

“Historically, expatriates have not been significant targets for kidnappings in the country. When kidnappings do occur, they often involve members of the Asian business community rather than foreign travellers or residents.”

Osman, who is originally from Leicester, worked for a local audit firm and had lived in Malawi with her husband and children for several years. Before her rescue, her family said they had not had any news of her, including any contact from the kidnappers demanding a ransom.

Her husband, Nazil Osman, told the local news outlet Nyasa Times: “I don’t know where she is or how she is. My wife is an auditor, and I have no issues with anyone.”

Her brother told the Sun on Tuesday: “My sister has been missing for five days with no trace or call,” adding that the family could not think of a motive for her kidnapping.

Police did not say whether information received in response to the offered reward had led to Osman’s rescue, adding that investigations were ongoing and more details would be shared “in due course”.

world.title: Louisiana firefighters find feline native to sub-Saharan Africa while responding to house fire
world.snippet: The African serval, illegally enclosed in the back yard, was subdued and transferred to an animal welfare facility Louisiana firefighters...
world.content:
Louisiana firefighters responding to a small house blaze found a wildcat native to sub-Saharan Africa illegally enclosed in the back yard, prompting an animal welfare agency to seek placing the creature in an appropriate environment, according to officials.

Firefighters investigating a report of a minor fire at a home in the suburban New Orleans community of Marrero on Tuesday spotted the cat in question – an African serval – behind the residence in a chain-linked enclosure resembling a cramped baseball batting cage, a spokesperson for the local animal protection services said.

A statement from Jefferson protection and animal welfare services (JPaws) said its director, Michelle Brignac, and humane department supervisor, Victoria Clark, joined firefighters at the scene after they were summoned there. Local laws in effect in Marrero require an exotic animal permit to legally keep a serval as a pet, and the owner of the home at the center of the case did not have such a document, JPaws spokesperson John McCusker told the Guardian on Thursday.

The statement said Brignac and Clark therefore “subdued the hissing serval and wrangled it” into a transport carrier from its 9ft-by-9ft (7.53-sq-meter) cage that McCusker likened to “a dog kennel”. Brignac and Clark then brought the serval to the JPaws facility in the nearby community of Harvey, according to the statement from the agency, which also shared vivid photographs of the wildcat.

Beside their black spots, svelte physiques and striking facial features, servals are known for their ability to leap as high as about 7ft (2 meters) in the air. So McCusker said JPaws gave the serval an entire room to itself while the agency sought an appropriate refuge for the wildcat, which was born in captivity but whose natural habitat is African grasslands.

Servals share some similarities with domesticated cats that make them immensely popular as pets, including their affinities for grooming themselves, purring, yowling and stalking potential prey.

Nonetheless, they are not easily sustained pets, JPaws’ statement maintained. Servals in captivity do not have the physical space and stimulation needed to engage in normal, healthy behaviors, and they endure chronic stress as a result, the agency’s statement said.

They mark their territory, become aggressive as they mature, cannot be fully house-trained and destroy furniture, and they have been known to barge through walls and doors, according to JPaws. Experts also say servals require a diet and specialized care beyond what house cats need, making them a major responsibility.

A social media post on Friday by Brignac said JPaws had managed to place the serval with a zoo “where he could have something very different: space, enrichment, appropriate care and an environment designed with his needs in mind”. Brignac’s post did not specify to which zoo she was referring.

The Marrero serval was the latest of several indicators of the wildcats’ growing popularity, a boom driven in part by social media content creators showing them in videos online.

Cases involving servals have also tended to generate widely read news headlines in North America.

That happened in Ohio in 2023, when officials in the Cincinnati area captured an African serval named Amiry that was spotted in a Cincinnati neighborhood tree and later tested positive for cocaine.

In late 2025, a search for an African serval that escaped a Pennsylvania wildlife center culminated in heartbreak after a motorist fatally struck the wildcat, as Philadelphia’s NBC News affiliated reported.

And the news outlet People reported on authorities in the Canadian city of Vancouver returning an African serval to its owners after it escaped and nestled under a neighbor’s porch in June.

The British Columbia province to which Vancouver belongs had just banned keeping exotic cats such as African servals as pets. But, People reported, the owners of such cats were given until the beginning of May 2027 to apply for permits to legally possess them.

world.title: ‘We demand the truth’: Olga Tokarczuk and JM Coetzee lead calls for proof of life of disappeared Eritrean writers
world.snippet: More than 180 writers sign letter renewing calls for information on 12 authors detained incommunicado since 2001 crackdown on free speech...
world.content:
More than 180 writers have signed a letter to Eritrean president Isaias Afwerki calling for proof of life for 12 writers arrested in 2001.

Nobel laureates Olga Tokarczuk and JM Coetzee join prominent writers including Colm Tóibín, Elif Shafak, Isabel Allende, Ben Okri, Yann Martel, Kamila Shamsie and Tsitsi Dangarembga in signing the letter organised by PEN International and dated 18 September, marking 25 years since a government crackdown on the independent press. “Within days, Eritrea’s free press and the nation’s independent voices were systematically crushed,” opens the letter.

It lists 12 writers who have been held incommunicado since 2001, including the poet Amanuel Asrat and playwright and journalist Dawit Isaak.

“The families of these writers, the Eritrean people and the global literary community have been met with a painful and unlawful silence,” continues the statement. “To withhold all information regarding their health, location, and survival is a violation of international law and an act of cruelty.”

Along with Asrat and Isaak, the other writers named in the letter are Dawit Habtemichael, Fessehaye “Joshua” Yohannes, Mattewos Habteab, Medhanie Haile, Sahle “Wedi-ltay” Tsegazeab, Said Abdelkadir, Said Idris “Abu Are”, Seyoum Tsehaye, Temesgen Ghebreyesus and Yousif Mohammed Ali. Six of the writers were profiled in the Guardian in 2015.

The letter, signed by 188 writers in total, calls for “immediate, verified proof of life for all arbitrarily detained Eritrean writers and critics”.

Other signatories include Andrei Kurkov, Anthony Doerr, Chloe Aridjis, Lauren Groff, Lemn Sissay, Maaza Mengiste, Madeleine Thien, Margaret Busby, Max Porter, Philippe Sands, Preti Taneja, Tice Cin and Viv Groskop.

“Mr President, Eritrea’s future must be built with its brightest minds, not based on their suppression,” the letter adds. “No writer or journalist should be disappeared for peacefully expressing their views.”

Eritrea operates as a repressive dictatorship under Afwerki, with no national elections held since independence in 1993.

“We remain in solidarity with our missing colleagues, and we will not cease our efforts until they are free,” the letter concludes.

Earlier this year, PEN International launched a petition, open to the public, which also calls for proof of life.

“Twenty-five years is an unbearable length of time for any family to live without knowing whether a loved one is alive,”, said Burhan Sönmez, president of PEN International. “These writers have not disappeared from our memory. We will continue to speak their names, and we will continue to demand the truth about what happened to them.”
